findings.title: Fires on reports of realized accidents, injuries, drownings, and deaths, especially incidents involving water or other immediate physical hazards.
Fires on preventive safety guidance and descriptions of potential hazards or risks, rather than accounts of harm that has already occurred.
Favors nonfinite participial or gerund forms—often -ing phrases modifying a noun or adding an action—rather than verbs serving as the main finite predicate.
Favors finite predicate verbs that state what a subject does or has, often in present or past tense, with a few incidental noun or heading uses.
Fires on elements that join or separate components: the conjunction “and” links times, while an underscore separates parts of an identifier.
Mostly fires on numerical ratings, fractions, and proportions, though several punctuation and word-fragment examples do not fit that pattern.
Fires on “of” linking a noun to its content, source, quality, purpose, or complement, especially in abstract or descriptive noun phrases.
Fires on “of” in time-span expressions such as “a day of activities,” “an evening of fun,” or “three days of talks.”
Marks separators or successive items in compact enumerations, especially adjacent score values in sports results.
The firings land on unrelated name fragments, punctuation, and markup, with no consistent shared function apparent.
Fires on email and forum reply-subject prefixes, especially “Re:” or “RE:”, with occasional related thread-header contexts.
The marked tokens range from SQL and sports terms to complementizers, citations, and news vocabulary, with no clear shared pattern.
Examples cluster around cooking and cold-water instructions, but also classroom-response terminology, insurance coverage, and travel vocabulary, with no clear shared function.
The firings span character and author names, houses and places, social roles or status, and software terms, without a reliable common pattern.
Fires in factual prose introducing or describing quantitative details, including measurements, financial amounts, dates, statistical rates, and formal identifiers.
Fires around numeric ranges and result-count or pagination formats, especially item listings such as “Showing 1–3 of 3.”
Fires on orthographically unusual or fragmented tokens—especially Greek/non-Latin text, URL or code fragments, and odd word-boundary pieces—rather than a shared subject.
Fires on ordinary Latin-script English words or word fragments embedded in prose; the snippets span unrelated topics, with no clearer semantic theme.
Fires around descriptions of organizations being founded or established and their founders, staff, or band lineups, across company and music profiles.
Strongly marks contact-person and key-people metadata, but also appears on unrelated sports scores, match statistics, and player references.
Fires mainly on Christian and biblical material—Jesus, salvation, Revelation, and scriptural exegesis—with occasional unrelated names or words.
Fires mainly on physical ground and walking surfaces, including pavement, floors, cracks, holes, and terrain; a few examples appear unrelated.
Favors precise historical or recurring milestones—sports titles, deadlines, seasons, annual events, and quantified records—rather than isolated everyday time references.
No stable semantic target is clear: the marked common words occur across personal blogs, food and travel copy, and generic descriptions.
Mostly country- and region-focused reporting about public life, development, tourism, and local business, especially in smaller nations; the legal excerpts are less clearly related.
Includes economic and financial reporting alongside unrelated chemistry, Linux, travel, climate, and celebrity passages, with no clear shared topic.
Marks contrastive turns that replace, qualify, or correct an expectation, often through “instead,” “rather,” “but,” “only,” or “actually.”
Often marks negation or exclusion, especially “not” constructions that reject an option or distinguish what something is from what it is not.
Marks explicit sameness, exact matching, or close likeness, with a few related cases describing what something is based on or derived from.
Marks looser parallels and shared features—similarities, recurring themes, or resemblance across different things—rather than exact identity.
The firings are heterogeneous, though “step-” family compounds recur (stepsister, stepbrother, step-father) among unrelated word fragments, abbreviations, and numbers.
Most marked spans are compact acronyms, initials, codes, or proper-name fragments (WOD, HGP, LAUP, FWPD, SOG, RIM, PM, MAP).
Fires mostly on ordinary word tokens and punctuation in fluent prose; the examples span unrelated subjects, with no clear narrower semantic role.
Fires mainly on numerals, dates, and price-like strings, often alongside fragments of larger words or structured listings; a broad formatting/tokenization tendency, not a topic.
Fires on the final digit of time-of-day timestamps, especially minute values, with an occasional similar terminal digit in a price.
Fires on punctuation and spacing used as boundaries in citations, bibliographic lists, and wiki-style structured text.
Fires on proper names and named entities—especially places, surnames, and organizations—rather than ordinary vocabulary.
Fires on ordinary lexical or grammatical material, including word fragments, in contrast to the positive pole’s proper-name pattern.
Fires on public-facing institutional and organizational writing—announcements, reports, professional updates, and discussion of organizational development—across otherwise varied fields.
Fires on a mix of specialized professional-service and legal-practice language, Catholic/Vatican material, and oilfield terminology, without a clear shared theme.
Marks wording that introduces a definition, label, or explanatory restatement, often with parenthetical quoted terms or constructions such as “known as” and “called.”
The examples span unrelated ordinary grammatical contexts—prepositions, articles, and a verb—with no clear shared semantic or discourse pattern.
Fires mainly on political authority and governance—rulers, prime ministers, officials, sovereignty, and the civil or executive powers of the state.
Fires on two apparently unrelated clusters: music and musical works or performances, and hotel-room amenities such as irons and hair dryers.
Fires around phrase-level collocations and idiomatic completions, especially prepositional phrases such as “in favor,” “in check,” “under the bus,” and “more of a.”
Fires mainly on relational function words in noun phrases and familiar expressions, especially “of” constructions, as in “jaws of defeat” and “picture of paradise.”
